meta.titre: Sartre's Atheistic Existentialism: why there is no given human nature and what follows from freedom
meta.sous_theme: Sartre: existence precedes essence, freedom and bad faith

sections.contenu_markdown: A young person in Douala is torn between a family expectation to study medicine and a personal wish to become a musician. Parents, teachers and friends all give advice, but who finally decides? Jean-Paul Sartre argued that the decision is yours, because no God, tradition or human nature has settled in advance who you are. That claim is the centre of his atheistic existentialism and appears again and again in GCE questions, both as short interpretation items and as full essays.

items: Existentialism is a philosophy that begins with the concrete experience of the individual who exists, chooses and acts.
Theists believe that God exists and is the creator; atheists deny that God exists.
Essence means what a thing is, the qualities that make it the kind of thing it is; existence means that it is.

sections.titre: Sartre: existence precedes essence, freedom and responsibility
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Atheistic existentialism
Sartre, a twentieth-century French philosopher, divided existentialists into Christian and atheistic thinkers and placed himself in the second group. He is an atheist because he denies that God exists, and his philosophy works out what follows for human beings. His lecture *Existentialism is a Humanism* gives the most accessible account.

### Existence precedes essence
Sartre's example is a paper-knife. An artisan who makes it first has a concept of it, its purpose and its method of production, so its **essence** comes before its **existence**. The traditional religious view treats God as a divine artisan with a concept of the human being, so that each person realises a fixed human nature. Sartre argues that if there is no God there is no designer and no pre-existing concept of the human being. A human being first exists, appears in the world, and only afterwards defines himself or herself through choices and actions. In his words, a human being is nothing but what he or she makes of himself or herself.

### Consequences
| Idea | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Freedom | With no given nature and no ready-made values, we are radically free; Sartre says we are condemned to be free, because we cannot escape choosing, and even refusing to choose is a choice |
| Responsibility | By choosing for myself I also affirm an image of what a human being should be, so I am responsible for my choices and in a sense for all humanity |
| Anguish | The awareness of this heavy responsibility |
| Abandonment | There is no God to rely on and no ready-made values to excuse us |
| Despair | We must act without counting on a guaranteed outcome |
| Bad faith | Self-deception: pretending that we are not free, for instance by hiding behind a role or saying "I had no choice" |

Sartre starts from **subjectivity**, the point of view of the individual consciousness, and calls his position a humanism because the human being is the source of value.

### Criticisms
Critics say that without God or a universal standard morality becomes arbitrary; that Sartre underestimates biology, upbringing and society; and that Christian thinkers need God to ground human dignity. Sartre replies that our situation limits our options but does not decide for us, and that freedom brings responsibility, not licence.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked what "existence precedes essence" means
variantes.contenu_markdown: Answer in three moves: contrast with the paper-knife (essence first); state that humans have no predetermined nature; conclude that people make themselves through free choices for which they are responsible.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the command word is critically examine or evaluate
variantes.contenu_markdown: Plan: exposition; arguments in favour (human beings do change their lives by choice; responsibility is taken seriously); criticisms (arbitrary morality; neglect of conditioning); Sartre's reply; reasoned judgement.

sections.enonce_markdown: Explain why Sartre thinks that the absence of God makes human beings completely responsible for what they become.

etapes.justification: The command word "explain" calls for reasons linking the absence of God to responsibility.
etapes.resultat_markdown: I must connect: no God, then no given nature, then freedom, then responsibility.

etapes.justification: It is Sartre's main illustration of the role God would play.
etapes.resultat_markdown: A craftsman has a concept before making the object; if God were a creator he would have a concept of the human being.

etapes.action: State the atheist premise and its result.
etapes.justification: This is the pivot of the argument.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Without God there is no designer or concept, so the human being has no given nature: existence precedes essence.

etapes.justification: These are the consequences the question asks for.
etapes.resultat_markdown: With no preset nature or values, I define myself by what I choose; I cannot blame God, nature or fate, and choosing for myself affirms an image of humanity.

etapes.justification: Anguish shows how the responsibility is felt.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The heavy responsibility produces anguish and abandonment. Therefore, for Sartre, the human being alone answers for what he or she becomes.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Model answer, key points: (1) The paper-knife has an essence before its existence because an artisan designs it. (2) If God existed as a designer, humans would also have a given nature. (3) Sartre denies God, so human existence comes first and essence is made by choice. (4) Humans are therefore free and cannot appeal to nature, fate or God as an excuse. (5) Choosing for oneself involves an image of humanity, hence responsibility and anguish.

items.erreur_markdown: Reversing the formula and attributing "essence precedes existence" to Sartre.
items.pourquoi_faux: That is the traditional picture, in which a creator's concept comes first; Sartre states the opposite for human beings.
items.correction_markdown: For Sartre existence precedes essence: humans first exist and have no predetermined nature; they define themselves through their choices.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that Sartre's freedom means doing anything without consequence.
items.pourquoi_faux: For Sartre freedom goes with responsibility and anguish.
items.correction_markdown: Freedom is the inescapable need to choose and to answer for what one chooses.

items.erreur_markdown: Explaining Sartre's atheism as a personal hatred of religion.
items.pourquoi_faux: The question is philosophical: Sartre denies that God exists and examines what follows.
items.correction_markdown: Atheism, for him, is the premise of the argument: without God there is no predetermined human nature.

items.erreur_markdown: Treating all existentialists as atheists, for example including Kierkegaard.
items.pourquoi_faux: Existentialism includes both theistic and atheistic thinkers.
items.correction_markdown: Sartre is atheistic, while Kierkegaard is a Christian existentialist.

items.enonce_markdown: Explain briefly the paper-knife example and what it is meant to show.
items.solution_markdown:
- A paper-knife is made by an artisan who first has a concept of it and its purpose, so its essence precedes its existence.
- Sartre uses it to show how the traditional religious picture treats humans: a creator with a concept of humanity.
- Without such a creator human existence comes first.
**Award a mark for each of the three points.**

items.enonce_markdown: Distinguish between anguish and bad faith in Sartre's thought and give an everyday example of each.
items.solution_markdown:
- **Anguish**: awareness of the weight of choosing and of the responsibility it carries. Example: a student realising that the course chosen will shape the whole life and that nobody else can choose it.
- **Bad faith**: pretending not to be free, which is self-deception. Example: a student who says "I had no choice, my parents decided" in order to avoid facing his or her own decision.
**Award marks for each definition and example.**

items.enonce_markdown: Sartre says that in choosing for myself I choose for all humanity. Evaluate this claim.
items.solution_markdown:
- Exposition: each choice expresses a view of what a human being should be, and others may follow it. Sartre illustrates with a young man who must choose between caring for his mother and joining a cause.
- Support: choices do set examples, and responsibility is real.
- Criticism: people differ, so there is no way to say that one individual choice speaks for everyone; there seems to be an inconsistency between radical freedom and universal responsibility.
- Judgement: the claim is persuasive as a statement about responsibility but unclear as a claim about universal standards.
**Award marks for exposition, an illustration, a criticism and a judgement.**

items_markdown: Sartre is an atheistic existentialist: he denies that God exists and works out the consequences for human beings.
Existence precedes essence: a human being first exists and then defines himself or herself through choices; there is no preset human nature.
The paper-knife shows the traditional picture in which a creator's concept comes first.
Freedom, responsibility, anguish, abandonment and despair follow; bad faith is the denial of one's freedom.
Do not equate all existentialists with atheism; Kierkegaard is a Christian existentialist.
For critical questions give exposition, support, criticisms (arbitrary morality, neglect of conditioning), Sartre's reply and a judgement.
